# Independent audit of quantitative uncaptured-fiber Doignon thresholds

Audited `candidate af89470c3209e9d8`, including
the intrinsic dimension argument, strict comparison in the selected
cap sum, counting case, and convex root-threshold extension.


finite-cover bounds depending on the actual volume distribution;
they do not supply the arbitrary-distribution OC constant.

1. If positive q-dimensional remainders are Minkowski-interpolated
at an integer target, the target fiber has dimension at least q and
at most the maximal intrinsic dimension q. All source direction
spaces must therefore coincide. This justifies applying normalized
q-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski even when original affine fiber
orientations vary. Compact inner approximations retain STRICTLY
negative cap margins; closed-cap boundary mass is not reassigned.

2. For q=0 every nonempty fiber is a singleton and every positive
remainder is that singleton. An integer convex combination preserves
strict negativity and is the unique point of its target fiber.
Thus the lattice-convexity assertions remain valid, including this
counting case and lower-dimensional original intersections.

3. F(t)=sum(w_z-t)_+ is strictly decreasing on [0,W), so the stated
t_* is unique when 0<mB<M. The Doignon selection gives for each
fiber a STRICT captured-mass inequality c_i(z)>w_z-t_*. Summing
over selected caps dominates the positive part fiberwise. At least
one w_z>t_* because F(t_*)=mB>0, so the total inequality really is
strict. This contradicts at most m caps of mass at most B. B=0
is separately and correctly handled by nonnegativity on every fiber.

4. The common-remainder conclusion does not assert any common point
in those remainders. The subsequent centroid choice uses only that
the original caps cover the fiber. Intrinsic Grünbaum supplies the
stated captured fraction, while the common absolute remainder makes
the chosen cut proper. The q=0 cover contradiction is immediate.

5. The explicit maximum-fiber-volume bound, its nearly equal-volume
consequence, and the implicit bound with B/gamma_q all have the
correct monotonicity direction. Their trivial mB>=M branches are
valid. The equal-weight specialization of the implicit bound
improves the heavy-fiber estimate exactly when N>=m, as stated.

6. A convex root threshold works because the remainder root at an
integer target dominates the weighted source roots, and a convex
threshold at that target is bounded above by the corresponding
weighted threshold values. No unsampled root-concavity assertion is
needed. Strictness is supplied by multiplying the threshold by
1+epsilon, or by the displayed eta addition; the finite-sum limit
then restores equality cases. Positivity is needed at the integer
bases being compared; the stronger initial positivity on conv(P)
is harmless. Vertical or intrinsically constant cap restrictions
are already covered by the strict-remainder argument.

7. The final relative-fraction counterexample has exact fiber
lengths (1,4,1), strict uncaptured lengths (1,1,1), and a convex
lower boundary 3|z|-3. Thus it correctly excludes relative-fraction
lattice-convexity without contradicting the absoluteresearch-agent bounds.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
